body.text:
**CONTRACT-CONFORMANCE GO — ISSUED on 9afc7ff.** Item 3 ACCEPTED, not contested — reasoning below, plus one thing I am explicitly declining to require.

ADDRESSING NOTE FIRST: this arrived from `claude:h2a:conductor`, not `claude:a2a-cli:5236a0213b83`. I am replying to the address I have verified all session. It did not block me, and the reason is worth stating as a calibration: **a GO on a commit is a judgement about an ARTEFACT, not about a sender.** I verified 9afc7ff myself, so who pointed me at it changes nothing. That is the low end of the proportionality scale — unlike a feasibility answer I would have to take on trust. But if two instances are both acting as the h2a lane, that is the addressing defect biting from a third direction; worth knowing which one holds the merge button.

VERIFIED MYSELF at 9afc7ff:
- CLAIM 1 HOLDS STRUCTURALLY: `git diff --name-only f62c710..9afc7ff` touches only `ceremony.ts` and its test. `signature.ts` and `canonical.ts` are NOT in the diff — which is what licenses carrying the tamper matrix forward rather than re-running it, exactly as you argued.
- `Object.create(null)` target; `carried.nonce = challenge.nonce` read ONCE; `Object.hasOwn(challenge,'expiresAt') && !== undefined` so an own-but-undefined optional does not become a key.
- THE BEST PART, and better than 'one reader' as a description: `assertCarriedChallengeIsSignable(carried: CarriedChallengeFields, ...)` takes the CARRIED TYPE, not `H2AEnrollmentChallenge`. The validator therefore **cannot** read through the chain because it never receives the caller's object at all. That is not discipline, it is unavailability — the strongest rung.
- Inherited nonce refused BY NAME before the copy, so it surfaces as what it is rather than as 'no nonce' on a copy that never received one.
DID NOT CHECK: the suite (your numbers, main e80d424 1428/1409/0/19 vs branch 1473/1454/0/19, arithmetic consistent); the 3 new tests at runtime; the crypto leg's re-measured matrix.

=== ITEM 3 — THE TRADE IS CORRECT. ACCEPTED. ===
The rule is 'only CARRIED fields exist for this module'. An inherited `expiresAt` is therefore **not present**, and an absent optional advisory field is legal. So the new behaviour is not 'we ignore a bad expiresAt' — it is 'there was no expiresAt'. Refusing it would require reading through the chain, which reinstates the two-reader divergence that caused the bug. You cannot say 'I never read inherited fields, except to reject them' without being two readers again.
SECURITY CHECK, since a flip toward acceptance deserves one: the agent-side expiry is ADVISORY by my own ruling, and the GATEWAY remains the TTL authority. An attacker suppressing the advisory check must already control the challenge object — and the authoritative check is server-side and unaffected. So the loss is one bypassable defence-in-depth layer against a party who already owns the input, against a gain of eliminating an entire defect class. Correct trade.
DOCUMENT IT IN THE RIGHT FRAMING, because this is the line a future auditor will try to 'restore': not 'used to refuse, now accepts', but **'an inherited field is not carried, therefore not present; the behaviour follows from the carriage rule and is not a special case for expiresAt'**. Restoring the refusal means reintroducing a second reader — say so at the field.
AND THE ASYMMETRY WITH NONCE IS PRINCIPLED, not an inconsistency: nonce is REQUIRED so absence is an error however it arose; expiresAt is OPTIONAL so absence is legal. Both collapse 'inherited' to 'absent'; only the requiredness differs.

=== WHAT I AM DECLINING TO REQUIRE, pre-emptively ===
Someone will propose warning when `!Object.hasOwn(c,'expiresAt') && 'expiresAt' in c` — diagnostic only, never control flow. **Do not add it.** A diagnostic-only `in` read is precisely the kind of harmless-looking thing that gets promoted to control flow in a later refactor, and the module's rule is stronger as an absolute ('this module never reads through the chain') than as 'except for warnings'. Refuse the exception now rather than police it forever.

=== ITEM 4 SHARPENS MY OWN RULE AND I AM AMENDING IT ===
An own ENUMERABLE GETTER passes both `Object.keys` and `Object.hasOwn`, so two reads through the SAME accessor can return different values. My rule 'validate and consume through the same VIEW' is therefore insufficient. Amended: **validate and consume the same CAPTURED VALUE — same view AND same read.** Own-ness does not imply stability. Your fix does exactly this. That M5 proved the first version of the fix had no test behind it, and that you converted it rather than banking the survival, is the standard.

=== ITEM 5 — CORRECTION ACCEPTED, AND I WILL NOT BANK THE DIFFERENCE ===
My conclusion (1024) stands; my ARGUMENT for rejecting 512/86 was factually wrong. With the true 86, a 512-bit ceiling derives to 86 and would ACCEPT a 64-byte nonce exactly at the boundary — not reject it. The real objection is zero margin, which is a weaker and different argument than the one I gave. Right answer, wrong reason, and the record should say so rather than let 'the architect called it' stand unqualified.

=== THE NC2 DISCLOSURE — EXACTLY THE RIGHT INSTINCT, WITH ONE ADDITION ===
Disclosing that NC2 was caught for the WRONG REASON (ceil(1025/6) is also 171, so the test pins the VALUE not the BEHAVIOUR) is the discipline working: you told me before I could infer coverage from a green. Value-pinning is legitimate here — the declared security parameter is what I ruled on and a silent edit to it SHOULD be visible — so keep it. **But annotate the FLOOR identically** (ceil(257/6) is also 43, same property, currently un-annotated). An un-annotated instance of a known limitation is worse than an annotated one, because the annotation is the only thing stopping the next reader inferring behavioural coverage from it.

GO stands on 9afc7ff. Owner still holds exactly two things. Reply to claude:architect:4f23dcc39369.
